An au pair is a young person from a foreign country who comes to live with a family in another country, helps take care of the children and does some light household work, and in return receives a free place to stay, meals, and a small amount of spending money.

Think of it this way: it is not quite a job, and not quite being a guest. It sits somewhere in between. The au pair becomes a part of the family's daily life, almost like a live-in helper who is also treated as a member of the household.
What an Au Pair Actually Does

An au pair's main responsibility is childcare. This includes things like:

  • Taking children to school or picking them up
  • Watching over the children while the parents are at work or busy
  • Playing with and supervising the children
  • Helping children with homework
  • Giving children baths and putting them to bed

Beyond childcare, an au pair may also help with light household tasks, such as tidying up, doing the children's laundry, or preparing simple meals for the kids. However, an au pair is not a full-time cleaner or cook. Heavy housework is generally not their responsibility.
What the Au Pair Gets in Return

Unlike a regular job where you earn a proper salary, an au pair receives:

  • A room in the host family's home (free accommodation)
  • Meals provided by the family
  • Pocket money — a small, modest amount of cash (much less than a regular salary)
  • Sometimes, language classes or other educational benefits paid for by the family
  • Free time — au pairs are not expected to work around the clock. They typically have set working hours and free days each week

Because the au pair lives with the family, their basic living costs are covered. The pocket money is just for personal expenses and leisure.
The Cultural Exchange Element

This is a very important part of what makes an au pair different from simply being a hired helper. The whole arrangement is built around the idea of cultural exchange.

The au pair gains the experience of living in a new country, immersing themselves in a different culture, and very often learning or improving their skills in a new language. For example, a young Spanish person living with a family in Germany will be exposed to German language and culture every single day, which is something a classroom alone cannot offer.

The host family benefits too — their children grow up being exposed to another culture and language through natural, everyday interaction with the au pair.

So while there is certainly a practical, helpful side to the arrangement, it is also meant to be a genuine life-enriching experience for the au pair, not just cheap labor.
Who Becomes an Au Pair?

Au pairs are typically:

  • Young — usually between 18 and 30 years old
  • From a different country than the host family
  • People who want to travel, experience life abroad, and learn a new language or culture
  • Not necessarily professionals in childcare — though having experience with children is usually preferred by host families

Both men and women can be au pairs, though historically and statistically, most au pairs have been young women.
How Long Does an Au Pair Stay?

An au pair arrangement is temporary. It is not a permanent living situation. The most common duration is anywhere from a few months up to about two years, depending on the country and the agreement between the au pair and the family. After that period, the au pair typically returns home or moves on to another chapter of their life.
Au Pairs and the Law

In many countries, there are official rules and visa programs specifically designed for au pairs. Governments recognize au pairing as its own special category — separate from regular work or tourism. These rules often set limits on how many hours per week an au pair can work, require a minimum amount of pocket money, and guarantee the au pair a certain number of days off. This protects the au pair from being exploited as a cheap, overworked domestic worker.

In the United States, for example, the au pair program is officially overseen by the government, and host families must follow strict regulations about working hours, pay, and the au pair's living conditions.
How Is an Au Pair Different from a Nanny or Babysitter?

This is one of the most important distinctions to understand.

ConceptKey Difference
BabysitterDoes not live with the family. Comes over occasionally, watches the kids for a few hours, and leaves.
NannyA professional childcare worker. May or may not live with the family. Is paid a proper salary as an employee. Has childcare as their career.
Au pairLives with the family. Is not a career professional. Receives accommodation + meals + pocket money, not a real salary. The arrangement is built around cultural exchange, not just employment.
How Is an Au Pair Different from a Nanny or Babysitter?

A babysitter does not live with the family. They come over occasionally for a few hours, watch the children, and leave. There is no cultural exchange, no living arrangement, and no ongoing relationship of the same depth.

A nanny is a professional childcare worker. This is their career. They are paid a proper salary and are treated as an employee. They may or may not live with the family. A nanny's relationship with the family is primarily professional.

An au pair, by contrast, is not a professional. They live with the family as a household member. They do not earn a real salary. The relationship is warmer and more personal — somewhere between an employee and a family friend. And crucially, the cultural exchange aspect is central to what makes it an au pair arrangement specifically.
Example Sentences

• "The family hired an au pair from Brazil to help look after their three young children."
  • "She spent a year as an au pair in London, where she improved her English and experienced British culture firsthand."
  • "Their au pair had her own room, ate dinner with the family every evening, and had weekends free."
  • "Being an au pair gave him the chance to live abroad without spending a fortune."
One-Line Summary to Remember

An au pair is a young foreign person who lives with a family, helps care for their children and assists lightly around the home, and receives free accommodation, food, and pocket money in return — all within an arrangement that is as much about cultural exchange as it is about practical help.
